Today I'd like to introduce a great place to eat in my neighbourhood. ‘Gohyangjip’ in front of the school is a hanjeongsik restaurant. Hanjeongsik is a traditional Korean meal, and a lot of dishes are served. I tried hanjeongsik for the first time here: there were many kinds of food, and many I had never seen before. **-찌개** is a thick stew (김치찌개, 된장찌개), **-탕** a soup (감자탕, 설렁탕, 삼계탕), **-찜** something braised or steamed (갈비찜), **-국수** noodles (칼국수, 비빔국수).
**달다** sweet · **짜다** salty · **맵다** spicy · **시다** sour · **쓰다** bitter. 맵다 is a ㅂ-irregular: 매워요, 매운 음식. 달다 drops ㄹ before ㄴ: 단 음식 (sweet food).

Put **중에(서)** after a noun to pick one out of a group, usually with **제일** or **가장** (the most): 한국 음식 **중에서** 불고기를 **제일** 좋아해요.

When the group is one place or one whole, use plain **에서**: 우리 반**에서** 유진 씨가 한국말을 제일 잘해요. 세계**에서** 제일 높은 산.

With close friends of the same age, younger people and family you drop **-요**: 가요 → **가**, 먹어요 → **먹어**, 좋아해요 → **좋아해**. After a noun: **(이)야** — 친구**야**, 학생**이야**. “Let's” is **-자**: 같이 먹**자**. 네 → **응**, 아니요 → **아니**, 저 → **나**, 제 → **내**.

How can we live a healthy life? Many people take expensive supplements or eat food that is good for the body. However, changing your daily habits matters more than that. Here are the healthy habits doctors talk about.
1. Laugh often and try to see the good side of everything.
2. Don't eat food that is too salty or spicy; eat more vegetables, fruit and fish than meat.
3. Do 30 minutes of light exercise every day. Exercising every day matters more than exercising for a long time at once.
4. Wash your hands as soon as you come home. Washing your hands often can prevent colds.
5. Always eat breakfast. A good breakfast is better for your health than a good dinner.

Many symptoms use **나다** (to come out, appear): 열이 **나요** (I have a fever), 기침이 **나요** (I'm coughing), 콧물이 **나요** (my nose is running), 몸살이 **났어요** (I ache all over). Others: 속이 안 좋아요 (my stomach feels bad), 어지러워요 (I'm dizzy), 기운이 없어요 (I have no energy), 입맛이 없어요 (I have no appetite).
**-약** and **-제** mean medicine: 감기약, 두통약, 멀미약, 안약; 소화제, 해열제. You **먹다** pills, **넣다** eye drops, **붙이다** a patch (파스), **바르다** ointment (연고).

In **낫다, 붓다, 짓다, 젓다** the final ㅅ **drops before a vowel**: 낫다 → 나**아**요, 나**았**어요, 나**으**면. Note that the vowels don't contract (나아요, not 나요). Before a consonant ㅅ stays: 낫**고**, 낫**지** 않아요. 벗다, 웃다, 씻다 are regular: 벗어요, 웃어요, 씻어요.
Hasn't your cold gone yet? — No, I'm still coughing.

**마다** after a noun: 아침**마다** (every morning), 주말**마다**, 사람**마다** (each person), 나라**마다** (each country). With a period of time it means “every …”: 여섯 시간**마다** (every six hours). 날마다 = 매일.
Culture differs from country to country.

**…아서/어서 왔는데요.** — I've come because… (the ending -는데요 sounds softer and invites a reply). **어제 저녁부터 계속 아파요.** — It's been hurting since yesterday evening. **…(으)ㄹ 것 같아요** — I feel like I'm going to…: 토할 것 같아요.

Verb stem + **-기로 하다** — a decision or an arrangement with someone. It's nearly always in the past: 주말에 친구를 만나**기로 했어요** (I've arranged to meet a friend). A negative decision: 안 가**기로 했어요** / 가**지 않기로 했어요**.

N을/를 위해서 = for (the sake of): 건강을 위해서 운동해요. 스트레스가 쌓이다 ↔ 풀리다: stress builds up ↔ goes away.

People's personalities can be divided into type E (extroverts) and type I (introverts). Type E people like talking and enjoy meeting new people. They sort out their thoughts while talking, and when stress builds up they talk to others. They tend to speak fast and loudly. Type I people don't talk much and feel uncomfortable meeting strangers. They speak after sorting out their thoughts, and when stress builds up they spend time alone. They tend not to show their inner feelings. So E types think I types are ‘hard to read’, and I types think E types ‘talk a lot’.

Adjective + **-아/어 보이다** is your impression from what you see: 기분이 좋**아 보여요** (you look happy), 피곤**해 보여요** (you look tired). Irregulars change as usual: 무겁다 → 무거**워 보여요**, 크다 → **커 보여요**, 어리다 → 어**려 보여요**.
Your bag looks heavy — shall I carry it?

**처럼** and **같이** after a noun mean “like, as if”: 가수**처럼** 노래를 잘해요 (sings well like a singer), 어른**같이** 말해요 (talks like an adult). They are interchangeable.
We've been like sisters since we were little.
**닮다** takes 을/를 or 하고, and is used in the **past** form for a present state: 저는 아버지**를 닮았어요** (I look like my father). 언니**하고** 얼굴이 **닮았어요**.
젊다 = young (an adult in their 20s–30s), 어리다 = young in the sense of a child or “younger than expected”: 어려 보여요 = you look young for your age.
Your bag looks heavy — shall I carry it?
Looking at this photo, you seem really happy.

My friend talks like a teacher.

A-(으)ㄴ 편이다 / V-는 편이다 — rather, tend to

**편** means “side”. Instead of a flat statement you say something is “on the … side”: 조용**한 편이에요** (I'm rather quiet). With verbs you need an adverb like 잘, 많이, 자주: 매운 음식을 **잘 먹는 편이에요** (I eat spicy food fairly well).
This restaurant tends to be crowded.

Chuseok, on the 15th day of the 8th lunar month, is an important Korean holiday. It is a day to thank the ancestors that the year's farming has ended well. On Chuseok morning people hold a rite with newly harvested grain and fruit and then go to visit the family graves. They make songpyeon and share it with neighbours, and have a good time talking with relatives they haven't seen for a long time. How Koreans write diaries, essays and news
In diaries, essays, newspapers and books Koreans don't write -아요/어요 or -습니다. They use the **plain style** ending in **-다**. In this style “I” is **나** (not 저) and “my” is **내**.

**Adjectives**: the dictionary form — 좋다, 어렵다, 많지 않다. **Verbs** (present): vowel stem + **-ㄴ다**, consonant stem + **-는다**: 가다 → **간다**, 먹다 → **먹는다**; ㄹ drops: 살다 → **산다**. **Nouns**: N**(이)다** — 학생이다, 가수다. **Past**: **-았다/었다** for everything — 갔다, 좋았다, 학생이었다. **Future**: **-(으)ㄹ 것이다**, **-겠다**.
I go to school at 8 every morning.
I read a book before going to sleep.
It's cool because the wind is blowing.
있다/없다 and -고 싶다 behave like adjectives: 있다, 없다, 가고 싶다. But -아/어하다 is a verb: 좋아한다.
